methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: How Windward turns Elexon's published wind data into a decision view and an accuracy record, and where its limits are.

sources.title: Data sources
body: Actual output comes from Elexon's FUELHH dataset, filtered to the WIND fuel type: metered generation from transmission-connected wind farms for every half-hour settlement period.

Forecasts come from Elexon's WINDFOR dataset: national wind generation forecasts published several times a day, each run covering roughly the next two days. Every run is kept with its publish time, so the forecast that was available at any moment can be reconstructed.

alignment.title: Aligning forecasts with actuals
body: Forecasts are hourly while actuals are half-hourly. Each hour's actual is the mean of its two half-hours, so both sides describe the same average power over the same hour.
An hour with only one of its two half-hours present is treated as incomplete and excluded from every error statistic rather than estimated.
alignment.sensitivity: Comparing only the half-hour that starts on the hour would lower the January gate-closure mean absolute error by about 18 MW, under 1%, so the alignment choice does not drive the results.

selection.title: Which forecast a trader actually had
body: Day-ahead power for GB is bought in auctions that close the morning before delivery, and each market has its own gate closure, listed under Scope of this pilot. For every delivery hour, Windward selects the latest forecast published before the chosen market's gate closure.

Forecast runs are published several times a day, so a run can land between two markets' deadlines. When that happens, buyers on different markets really had different forecasts; the decision desk shows which run each market had.
When the latest run before the deadline does not cover an hour, the value comes from the most recent earlier run that does, and the hour is flagged as coming from an older run.

band.title: Uncertainty range and energy at risk
body: The range around each forecast comes from the errors of comparable forecasts on the other pilot days. Hours are grouped by forecast level, because errors grow as wind output rises, and each group's range is the observed spread of its errors.

The edges use a finite-sample (conformal) correction, so a small calibration set does not make the range look tighter than it is. The lower edge is the level actual wind is expected to beat about nine times in ten: plan on that, not on the expected value. The decision desk reports how often it actually held across the pilot.
Energy at risk is the expected daily volume minus the firm daily volume. It is the amount a buyer relying on the forecast may have to cover in balancing.
Calibration leaves the day being assessed out of its own range, so the range is never fitted to the outcome it is judged against.

sign.title: Error sign convention
body: Error is forecast minus actual. A positive error, or a positive bias, means the forecast was too high: a buyer who planned on it bought too little and ends up short, paying balancing prices for the difference.
A negative error means the forecast was too low and the buyer ends up long.

caveats.title: Caveats
body: The pilot covers one winter month. Error statistics from a single month describe that month's weather and may not hold in other seasons.
FUELHH and WINDFOR describe transmission-connected wind only. Embedded wind on distribution networks appears as reduced demand and is outside this view.
The uncertainty range is calibrated on the days in the pilot window, so it inherits their weather regime and sample size.
Hours missing a forecast or an actual are excluded from statistics and flagged, never filled in.
